source.title: Distributional Generalization: A New Kind of Generalization

record.tranche_reason: The paper trains interpolating classifiers on structured label noise and measures whether the noisy label distribution is reproduced on test data. This bears on V4, but it does not test fully random labelings.
record.gate_note: The paper's random sparse confusion matrix and class-specific noise sweeps are its own results. The cited Zhang et al. result is prior work and is not recorded as a row. Other reported generalization results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own SGD-trained networks interpolating randomly corrupted labels and reproducing the corruption on test inputs. These results bear on V4 in a structured, class-conditional noise setting, without testing complete uniform random relabeling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors argue that interpolating classifiers often reproduce structured aspects of the training distribution in test predictions, and that memorization influences decision boundaries rather than acting like a simple lookup table. They present conjectures whose applicable distributions and classifier families remain incompletely specified.
record.recipe_differences: Uses standard interpolating training with noisy labels and train/test confusion distributions, rather than testing completely random labels and measuring chance test error.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that Feature Calibration depends on architecture and interpolation: the CIFAR-10 class partition works for WideResNet but not MLP, and early stopping changes the behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing L2 regularization prevents Gaussian kernel regression from fitting structured label noise on MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization can suppress structured-noise fitting in kernel classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 11 reports that a WideResNet fits progressively more structured label noise as training continues, with similar train/test confusion patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured-noise fitting increases with training duration and is mirrored in test predictions.

record.problems: The relevant label-noise experiments use structured corruptions rather than fully random labels. Test confusion matrices are shown in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were reported. Figure 10's Gaussian-kernel regularization sweep and Figure 11's WideResNet training-time sweep concern non-interpolating behavior and do not test fitting fully random labels.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, chance test accuracy, and fitting without changes to training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparisons between true and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Uniform random corruption spanning the entire dataset from none to all, and a full test-error trajectory ending at chance. R1 varies corruption within one class; R2 uses one sparse confusion matrix.

Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent deep networks from fitting completely random labels, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization. The kernel regularization experiment does not test this version.

A direct comparison establishing that shared real-label patterns are learned before noisy labels. Figure 11 reports increasing noise fitting over time, but the supplied text does not establish that ordering.

missing.what: The binary Animal/Object experiment trains WideResNet-28-10 to zero error after randomly flipping 30% of cat labels to Object; roughly 30% of test cats are likewise classified as Object while other classes remain largely unaffected.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the extracted limits_scope verdict: an untested uniform-noise regime and an unmeasured chance endpoint are coverage gaps, not demonstrated failures. No exact numerical test-confusion entries can be recovered from the supplied figure captions.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment trains on a completely random labeling of the training set.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed across label-noise fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Noise is structured: class-specific flips or a sparse confusion matrix, not uniform random relabeling across the training set. The paper does not report a full train/test error curve rising to chance.
No test of whether regularization, dropout, or augmentation prevents fitting fully random labels or affects true-label generalization in that setting.
No measurement of whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: WideResNet-28-10
rows.operation_detail: Trained to zero training error on CIFAR-10 with class 0 flipped to class 1 at varying probability p.

conditions.value: zero train error; hyperparameters described in Table 2

rows.measure: Test-set classifier outputs compared with the applied label-noise distribution
rows.baseline: Applied label-noise distribution on the train set
rows.value: Classifier outputs on the test set closely track the confusion matrix; Figure 4 varies p ∈ [0, 1].
rows.note: Reports a class-conditional flip sweep, not fully random labeling. No numerical error values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The result is correctly described, but p is the corruption probability within class 0, not across the whole dataset. Even p = 1 corrupts only approximately 10% of CIFAR-10. The zero-training-error evidence for this row is in D.4.1; excerpt E1 instead describes the separate binary Animal/Object experiment in D.2.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, Figure 4; Appendix D.4.1, pp. 31–32; Table 2.

rows.subject: WideResNet-28-10
rows.operation_detail: Trained to interpolation on CIFAR-10 with a random sparse confusion matrix applied to labels.

conditions.value: each class preserved with probability 50%; flipped to two other classes with probabilities 20% and 30%

rows.baseline: Train confusion matrix from the applied label-noise distribution
rows.value: Train and test confusion matrices are close and share the same sparsity pattern.
rows.note: The noise is structured by a sparse confusion matrix; exact matrix entries for test predictions are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: This is a single structured-noise condition with 50% label preservation, not a corruption-fraction sweep. Its test confusion matrix supports retained class signal and reproduced noise, but cannot establish a trajectory toward chance.
